newsitem.title: UK: Britain wants constructive talks with EU on beef ban.
newsitem.headline: Britain wants constructive talks with EU on beef ban.

text.p: The new Labour government, which has promised a fresh start in Britain's dealings with Europe, wants to work constructively to get a year-old EU ban on British beef exports lifted, Agriculture Minister Jack Cunningham said on Wednesday.

The ban, imposed by the European Union in March 1996 after British scientists uncovered evidence that BSE, or mad cow disease, could probably be transmitted to humans, will top the agenda when Cunningham meets European Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler in Brussels on Monday.

"Our urgent objective is an end to the beef ban and we need to map out in a much more constructive way how we believe that can be achieved in partnership with our European colleagues," Cunningham told BBC radio.

The previous Conservative government, after blocking EU business for a month to put pressure on its partners, agreed at last June's Florence summit on a framework for gradually lifting the ban. Nearly a year later, the ban remains in force.

"There's no good threatening beef wars, as we saw the last administration do. That made a difficult situation much worse, and if we can do this within the terms of the Florence agreement -- then fine," Cunningham said.

In a separate briefing on Tuesday, Cunningham acknowledged that progress would not be easy. But he said Prime Minister Tony Blair's intention that his government should be positive in its dealings with Europe would help.

"I don't want to give the impression that I am a starry-eyed optimist about it, but I think we will have a more constructive dialogue and in doing so will improve the chances of getting more of the kind of response we want to see," he said.
Cunningham told the BBC that a reform of the EU's Common Agricultural Policy was a "very very important issue" for the new government, from Blair down.

Cunningham said another task would be to restore his new ministry's morale, which has been battered by the crisis over BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) and an outbreak of E.coli food poisoning in Scotland that killed 20 people.

"Civil servants have had a difficult time. There have been a number of political failings -- I think that's a polite way to put it -- over the last two or three years in this department, which has meant it's rather a gloomy place in some respects," he said.
To draw a line under the past, Cunningham said he was thinking of changing its present title of Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food.

He said he had started reorganising the ministry to bring together those offices likely to be hived off into a new Food Standards Agency. Labour committed itself while in opposition to setting up such an agency to improve public health.
Cunningham is one of the very few Labour ministers with previous experience of government, having served as energy minister under Prime Minister James Callaghan in the 1970s.
In opposition he served as spokesman on the environment, trade and industry and, latterly, the national heritage.
